title: Field Sanitation - Military Standards
summary: U.S. Army field sanitation standards adapted for civilian grid-down camps: a sanitation team, latrine siting and types, hand-washing, waste water, flies and rodents, water discipline, and kitchen hygiene.

steps.title: Appoint a sanitation team
steps.body: The Army requires each company-sized unit to train a field sanitation team that inspects latrines, hand-wash stations, water, and food areas every day and reports problems to leaders. Do the same for a family or neighborhood camp: name two responsible people, give them authority, and rotate helpers. Their daily walk-through should check soap and water at every station, latrine depth and lids, standing water, trash, and anyone sick. Sanitation fails when it is everyone's job and no one's responsibility.

steps.title: Site latrines to Army standards
steps.body: Army field sanitation training places latrines at least 100 feet (30 m) from any water source, at least 100 yards (90 m) downwind of the food service area, and about 30 yards (27 m) from the edge of the living area. Put them downhill from wells and springs. Choose latrine type by how long you stay: cat holes about 1 foot (30 cm) deep for people on the move; straddle trenches about 1 foot wide, 2.5 feet deep, and 4 feet long for stays up to about 3 days; and deep pits with fly-tight box seats for longer. Details are in guide medical-009.

steps.title: Close latrines correctly
steps.body: Close a trench or pit when waste reaches within 1 foot (30 cm) of the surface or when you leave. Remove any seat box, then fill with soil in thin layers, packing it every few inches. Mound about 1 foot (30 cm) of soil above ground level to shed rain and keep flies and animals out. Post a marker with the latrine type and date. Proper closure prevents later digging accidents and keeps flies from breeding in the waste.

steps.title: Make hand-washing automatic
steps.body: Install a hand-washing device outside each latrine and near the kitchen, and keep it constantly supplied with soap and water - that is an Army standard, not a suggestion. A water jug with a spigot or a tippy-tap made from a jug and rope works well. Wash with soap for about 20 seconds before handling food, after latrine use, after caring for the sick, and after handling animals or trash. Do not share towels; air dry or use a personal cloth.

steps.title: Dispose of waste water and trash
steps.body: Pour wash and kitchen water through a grease or food trap into a soakage pit - a hole filled with rocks or rubble - well away from water sources. Large camps should rotate between two pits. Never dump gray water on the ground near living areas or into streams. Store trash in covered containers and bury or burn it daily well downwind, following local fire rules. Garbage left out draws flies, rodents, and larger animals.

steps.title: Control flies, mosquitoes, and rodents
steps.body: Keep latrine lids closed, cover all food, and remove breeding sites: standing water, open trash, and manure. Use EPA-registered repellents and bed nets, and keep food sealed and off the ground. Clean rodent droppings only by soaking them with disinfectant first, never by sweeping. See guide medical-010 for repellent choices and rodent cleanup steps.

steps.title: Enforce water and kitchen discipline
steps.body: Treat all drinking water by an approved method before use (see water-002 and water-003). Do not drink from shared pots or let people dip personal cups into the group container - pour instead. In the kitchen, wash, rinse, and sanitize dishes after every meal, cook food thoroughly, and serve it promptly. Anyone with diarrhea, vomiting, fever, or open sores on the hands must not cook or serve food for others. One sick cook can disable an entire camp.

warnings: A single sanitation failure - an empty soap station or a sick cook - can cause an outbreak that disables a whole group.
Never site a latrine uphill of or within 100 feet (30 m) of a water source.
Do not sweep or vacuum rodent droppings; soak them with disinfectant first.
Burning trash or waste near shelters creates toxic smoke and fire risk.
proTips: Put the hand-wash station on the path out of the latrine so washing is the easiest choice.
Use a simple daily checklist for the sanitation team and post it where everyone sees it.
Color-code containers: blue for drinking water, red for wash water, so they never get mixed.
Treat clothing and bed nets with permethrin before you need them, following the label.

whenNotTo: Do not dig pits in flood-prone ground or where the water table is shallow - use bucket toilets and haul waste.
Where working toilets or municipal sanitation still function, use them instead of field latrines.

quickGlance.situation: You are running a multi-person camp without working sanitation and need to prevent disease outbreaks.
immediate: Name a sanitation team to inspect latrines, wash stations, water, and kitchen daily
Site latrines 100+ ft from water and 100 yards downwind of food
Keep soap and water at every latrine and the kitchen at all times
then: Route gray water to a soakage pit; cover trash and food
Bar anyone with diarrhea, vomiting, fever, or hand sores from cooking
